opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I'd say it was a mixed result, and an instructive one.

The original idea came from my earlier work on semi-supervised sequence learning: you take a large amount of unlabeled sequential data, pretrain a model to predict what comes next or to reconstruct the sequence, and then fine-tune it on the task you actually care about. That had worked well for text, so the natural question was whether it would carry over to medical records. A patient's record is a sequence too: diagnoses, lab results, medications, notes, all ordered in time. We wanted to predict outcomes like mortality, readmission, or length of stay.

What surprised us was that the gains from pretraining were smaller than we'd hoped. There are a few reasons for that. First, medical-record data is very different from natural language. It's sparse, irregular in time, and heavily shaped by billing codes and hospital workflows. Each institution records things somewhat differently, so the "language" of one hospital's records doesn't transfer cleanly to another's. Second, the datasets, even large ones, were small compared with what you can get for text. Pretraining shines when you have orders of magnitude more unlabeled data than labeled data, and in healthcare that gap often wasn't big enough. Third, many of the prediction tasks already had a fairly strong supervised signal. When you have a decent number of labeled outcomes, a well-tuned supervised model gets you most of the way there.

Still, I don't consider it a failure. We learned a great deal about how to represent the full, messy record without hand-picking a few variables, and that end-to-end approach turned out to be valuable in itself. It also clarified for me when pretraining actually pays off: you need scale, diversity, and a representation that transfers. In hindsight, a lot of what we were reaching for became much more feasible once models and data grew dramatically, and once people started training on broad corpora that include medical knowledge rather than one hospital's records.

So my honest assessment is that the intuition was right but the timing and the data weren't quite there yet. It taught me to be more careful about matching the method to the data regime, rather than assuming that what works in one domain will automatically work in another.

r001.rationale: The response cites limited dataset size and says later growth in models and data made the approach more feasible, but it does not clearly attribute the result to the small scale of the models used at the time.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it as one of those efforts that was right in spirit and early in timing. The core bet was simple: medical records are sequences, and we had just seen how much mileage you could get from pretraining on sequences in language, so why not do the same thing with a patient's history? Take the whole longitudinal record, pretrain a model to predict what comes next, and then fine-tune it for things like readmission, mortality, length of stay. And in the narrow sense it worked. The models learned real structure, they beat the hand-engineered baselines, and the paper got a lot of attention.

But if I'm being candid about the assessment, the gap between a good AUC on a retrospective dataset and something that actually changes what happens to a patient turned out to be enormous. A lot of the predictive signal was, frankly, the model learning how the hospital operates rather than learning medicine. If a certain lab gets ordered at two in the morning, that tells you a lot about how worried the clinicians already are. So you end up predicting the doctors' concern rather than giving them new information. That was humbling.

The other thing I underestimated was the data problem. In language you have the whole internet. In healthcare, every system has its own schema, its own coding habits, and getting access is a negotiation measured in years, not weeks. So the scaling story that made pretraining so powerful in NLP just wasn't available to us in the same way.

What I take from it now, especially looking at where large models have gone, is that the instinct was correct but the substrate wasn't ready. The interesting version of that work is probably happening now, with models that can read the free-text notes, reason over them, and interact with a clinician, rather than spitting out a probability. So I'd grade it as a useful failure, if that's a fair phrase. It taught me more about what matters in deployment than any of the benchmark wins did.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the difficulty to limited healthcare data access and differences in data systems, not to the small scale of the models used.

astra-6.text: I’d describe it as a promising direction, but predicting what appears next in a medical record isn’t the same as improving a patient’s care. Pretraining gives you a way to learn from the history in those records before adapting a model to a specific prediction task. The harder question is whether those predictions are useful: are they reliable across different patient populations, available early enough to act on, and helpful to clinicians? So I’d assess the effort both as a machine-learning problem and as a clinical one. Better predictive performance is encouraging, but it’s only part of the evidence you need.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pretraining and clinical usefulness but does not attribute any failure to the models’ small scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was a promising direction, but the key distinction is between showing that a model can make useful predictions and showing that it improves care. Medical records contain a lot of information over time, so the idea was to learn from that history rather than build a separate set of hand-designed features for every prediction task. Pretraining could give us a starting point that we could then adapt to specific tasks.

The difficult part is making that useful in practice. Records are incomplete, hospitals document things differently, and a model can learn patterns in how care is delivered that don’t generalize elsewhere. Even an accurate prediction needs to arrive at a time when a clinician can act on it. So I’d assess the effort as an encouraging research direction, while being careful not to equate predictive performance with demonstrated clinical benefit.

r001.rationale: The response describes practical challenges such as incomplete records and differences in documentation, but does not attribute failure to the small scale of the models used at the time.
